[h1]I really wanted to enjoy this before jumping to Witcher 3, but...[/h1]

yes, I know I'm late to the party. But isn't that was recommendations are for?

Long story short, I played Witcher 2 for the first time ever in 2026, and it definitely hasn't aged well.

Why? Because it's clunky:
The controls don't feel good, combat is difficult to manage when you're fighting multiple enemies at once, and it just feels much more awkward than it should.

I've been gaming since 2007, and I've played plenty of older games. There are tons of games from around the same time, and even much older ones, that don't have these problems. So I don't think this is simply a case of the game being old or technology not being good enough back then.
Even in 2011, I don't see a good reason for combat to feel this clunky.

Maybe I would've enjoyed it more if I had played it back in 2011, but I still doubt it.

[h2]Combat Is the Biggest Problem[/h2]

The combat is what really makes me question whether I want to continue.

Fighting multiple enemies is unnecessarily difficult because it's hard to properly keep track of everything around you. I mean like blocking the attacks you want to block, or using spell from a distance. The whole system just feels awkward.

Another problem is what happens when you die:
it doesn't restart from the current fight. You have to defeat previous enemies again, and lots of times you have to keep rewatching cutscenes.

If I'm going to retry a difficult encounter, I don't want to spend my time repeating everything that came before it.

[h2]And Then There's Performance[/h2]

I'm also stuck around 60 FPS, which is pretty strange considering the age of the game and how it looks.

The graphics aren't exactly impressive by modern standards, so seeing the game struggle to go beyond 60 FPS in 2026 is not exactly reassuring.

It also makes me wonder just how poorly optimized this game must have been back in 2011.

[h2]Should You Just Play The Witcher 3?[/h2]

I own The Witcher…

I went into The Witcher 2 with high hopes.The combat is the biggest disappointment. It feels stiff and unresponsive in a way that constantly pulls you out of the moment. Light attacks, heavy attacks, dodges, and signs sound straightforward on paper, but the hitboxes are unreliable, animations lock you in place, and canceling moves is a nightmare. Fights against groups or bosses quickly turn into cheap, trial-and-error slogs rather than satisfying duels. I died far more often to clunky controls and stamina issues than to any real challenge. Compared to the first Witcher, it's even more button-mashing with extra frustration and even less flow.
The game also throws you in the deep end with almost no helpful tutorial, then punishes you harshly for not already knowing how everything works. The inventory and menus are cumbersome, the map is borderline useless in tighter areas, and the constant backtracking through linear zones gets tiring fast. Choices from the first game are mostly brushed aside or heavily railroaded, which makes your previous playthrough feel like it barely mattered. On top of that, bugs, crashes, and painfully long loading screens (even for simple doors) kept breaking any sense of immersion I had left.
The story has some genuinely strong moments and solid voice acting, but it’s bogged down by predictable plotting and lengthy exposition dumps. The endings feel rushed after all the buildup, and the world itself is smaller and less alive than I wanted—no real sense of open exploration, just corridors of rocks, trees, and political intrigue that never quite lands with the weight it aims for.
The Enhanced Edition smooths out a few rough edges, but it doesn’t fix the core jank. If you’re coming from The Witcher 3 or simply want smooth, rewarding gameplay, I’d recommend skipping this one. It has real narrative ambition, and that makes the disappointing mechanics sting even more. A rough middle chapter at best. Not recommended.

The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings is a massive leap forward from its predecessor. It delivers a mature, politically charged dark fantasy experience. Your choices radically reshape the entire narrative, making it a standout RPG.

Pros: 
Branching Narrative: Act 2 is entirely different depending on a choice you make in Act 1. You get two completely unique perspectives on the war.
Mature Storytelling: The plot avoids simple "good vs. evil" tropes. It focuses instead on complex grey morality and political realism.
Visual Design: The RED-engine delivers stunning environments, detailed character models, and incredible lighting that still holds up.
Preparation-Based Combat: Alchemy and traps matter. You must drink potions and oil your blade before a fight, rewarding tactical planning.
Memorable Characters: Compelling companions like Vernon Roche and Iorveth add deep emotional stakes to your decisions.

Cons:
Difficulty Spike: The prologue and early Act 1 are brutally punishing, even on normal difficulty. 
Clunky Navigation: The map system is confusing. Finding your way through multi-level zones like Flotsam or Vergen can be frustrating.
Targeting System: Combat targeting feels sticky and erratic when fighting large groups of enemies.
Abrupt Ending: Act 3 feels rushed and short compared to the expansive first two acts.

Final Verdict: 9/10. A must-play for RPG fans. It bridges the gap perfectly between the cult-classic original and the open-world masterpiece of The Witcher 3.

Review – The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings Enhanced Edition (Steam)

I played The Witcher 2 after finishing newer RPGs, and despite its age, it still stands out for its story, choices, and political intrigue.

👍 What I Loved

The story is excellent, with a darker and more mature tone than most fantasy RPGs.
Choices actually matter. Entire quest lines, locations, and perspectives can change depending on your decisions.
The characters are memorable, especially Geralt, Roche, Iorveth, and Triss.
The game respects your intelligence and doesn't constantly hold your hand.

👎 What Didn't Age Well

Combat can feel clunky and unforgiving, especially during the early chapters.
The UI and inventory management are dated.
Some quests don't always provide clear directions, which can lead to unnecessary confusion.
The game expects preparation before difficult fights, something that may frustrate players coming from The Witcher 3.

⚖️ Final Verdict
The Witcher 2 may not be as polished or accessible as The Witcher 3, but it offers one of the strongest stories and most meaningful choices in the RPG genre. If you can tolerate some dated mechanics, you'll find a fantastic adventure with consequences that genuinely matter.

Recommended 👍
A must-play for fans of story-driven RPGs and anyone who wants to experience one of Geralt's best adventures. ⭐⭐⭐⭐

I downloaded this game about three years ago and then completely forgot about it so last week I finally gave it a shot. I didn't really care for the game at first, but once I completed the prologue and started chapter 1, something clicked and I became hooked. I recommend watching a guide on this game when starting chapter 1, it really helped me understand the mechanics and how the different systems work. I watched a video from Ellie Menopy and it really helped how I approached combat, and the game's other mechanics, but to summarize: Use the Quen Sign. The graphics are a bit dated, but that's expected for a 15 year old game. However, the art style has a charm to it.

The Story: It's pretty good and as a fan of  the books I enjoyed the callbacks and references to them. It's not a requirement, but I definitely recommend giving the books a read, they're a treat. Anyways, the choices you make throughout the story really do matter and can affect what areas and NPCs you'll have access to.

Some negatives of the game are that the movement and combat can feel clunky early on, but once you upgrade certain skills the experience feels better. The main story is also pretty short, which can be great for replayability, but can catch you off guard. Another negative is prevalence of what I guess I would call "door loads" you have to walk through in zones. With the hardware from the time of release it's understandable why there's such a prevalence of them, but it can be a slight annoyance when going back and forth between areas.

I give the game a 7.5/10

citations.review_text: Many games are like playing a movie, but The Witcher 2 is like playing a novel. It's visually and mechanically dated but definitely worth playing for fans of the series. Smaller in scale than The Witcher 3, but that allows the writers to better integrate the side quests into the main quest, crafting a robust story. The divergent story paths after Act One make for a very rewarding narrative experience overall and give the game huge replay value. Graphics are PS3-era but at PS4 resolution, making for an interesting aesthetic; for instance, Geralt's costume details are sharp, water and wet sand look amazing, but some textures --especially rock faces--betray the wireframes underneath. Voice-acting is top shelf (although the main characters mysteriously have American accents while the supporting characters seem entirely European). Content-wise, if The Witcher 3 is a "soft R," The Witcher 2 would rate a hard R, featuring full female nudity and very coarse language (although the violence features no limb-lopping).

The Political Masterpiece
If the first game was a moody indie experiment, The Witcher 2 was the loud, confident statement that put CDPR on the map. Even today, it remains one of the most visually striking and narratively dense games ever made.

The Ultimate Branching Path: This game contains perhaps the boldest narrative choice in gaming history. At the end of Act 1, your decision completely changes Act 2—giving you two entirely different maps, quests, and perspectives. It is a game designed to be played at least twice.

The Combat Shift: Gone is the rhythmic clicking. Witcher 2 introduced the tactical, high-lethality action combat that would eventually be refined in Wild Hunt. You will roll, you will use traps, and you will die if you are careless.

The "Kingslayer" Plot: The story is tighter and more political than its successor. Hunting Letho through the fog of war provides a driving momentum that never lets up.

Verdict: 9.5/10 — A masterpiece of pacing and consequence.
